analysis.one_liner: Repealed critical habitat protections and required taxpayers to pay landowners for development blocked to protect species.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 229-193 on September 29, 2005 — 193 of 230 Republicans for, 158 of 202 Democrats against — but the Senate never voted, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Endangered Species Act: it repeals the government's authority to designate critical habitat, tells the Interior Secretary to list species only "sparingly" and to weigh the economic impact of each listing, weakens mitigation requirements, and treats pesticide use as automatically compliant with the law. It would also pay private property owners the fair market value of any development the Act blocks, give the President power to waive the Act for national security or after a disaster, and shift more power to states and local governments. It passed the House on a mostly party-line vote, then sat in a Senate committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Developers and industries whose projects run into protected species habitat would gain the most: the bill removes critical habitat designations, makes listing species harder, limits mitigation to what is "roughly proportional," and lets federal agencies measure harm only against a baseline that ignores past damage. Ranchers would get reimbursement for livestock lost to reintroduced predators, and pesticide users and makers would be deemed compliant with the Act simply by following pesticide-registration rules. Private landowners could claim taxpayer payments for the fair market value of foregone development, including business losses, and could receive annual conservation payments of up to 100% of their costs.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Secretary of the Interior's authority to designate critical habitat, the Endangered Species Act's main mechanism for protecting the places listed species live.
Directs the Secretary to list species only "sparingly" and to prepare an analysis of the economic and national-security impacts of each listing, adding hurdles to new protections.
Requires the government to compensate private property owners at the fair market value of a foregone use, including business losses, whenever the Act blocks a proposed use of their property.
Deems any action involving a pesticide that complies with federal pesticide law to automatically satisfy the Act's consultation and take-avoidance requirements.
Requires mitigation terms to be "roughly proportional" to the harm of an incidental taking and limits the government to requiring less-than-full-cost offsets in many cases.
Authorizes reimbursement of ranchers for livestock lost to reintroduced endangered or threatened species, without requiring them to present the dead animal.
Authorizes the President to waive the Act for national security and to suspend it in any area after a federally declared major disaster.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the new compensation, grant, and annual-payment programs, which pay owners the market value of development they can no longer pursue. The broader public would bear the cost in weakened protections for the habitats and species the current Act shields.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and the public's wildlife protections

drawbacks.text: Repealing critical habitat designation removes the Act's principal habitat-protection tool; habitat loss is the leading driver of extinction, so species would lose the protection of the places they live even while remaining on the list.
The "only sparingly" listing standard and the new economic-impact analyses could sharply reduce the number of species added to the protected lists.

Paying owners the fair market value of foregone development, including business losses, whenever the Act blocks a use would create potentially large, open-ended taxpayer payouts and could make protecting a species on private land expensive by design.
Treating pesticide-registered actions as automatically compliant ends federal review of pesticide harms to listed species, even where the pesticide registration never considered those species.

The "roughly proportional" mitigation standard and the requirement to analyze only new impacts beyond a pre-action baseline would let projects proceed while their cumulative harm to struggling species goes unaddressed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does contain genuine improvements: it would put species lists, recovery plans, and cost reports on public websites, set deadlines for recovery plans, pay livestock losses, and eliminate the little-used committee process for exempting agencies from the Act. But those items are narrow compared with the core effect: repealing critical habitat, making listings rare, capping mitigation, exempting pesticides, and obligating taxpayers to compensate owners for development the Act blocks. An honest reading is that a few useful provisions ride on a bill whose main effect is to make it harder to protect species and their habitat.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House 229-193, but the Senate never took it up — it sat in the Environment and Public Works Committee until that Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Pombo, chair of the House Natural Resources Committee, introduced the bill on September 19, 2005; the committee held hearings the next day, marked it up two days later, and reported it amended on a 26-12 vote within eight days.
The Rules Committee issued a rule allowing only 90 minutes of debate, considering the bill as read, and allowing only specified amendments.
The House passed the bill 229-193 on September 29, 2005 (Roll Call 506): 193 of 230 Republicans voted yes, while 158 of 202 Democrats voted no; 36 Democrats and 34 Republicans crossed party lines.
The Senate received the bill on September 30, 2005 and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, which took no further action before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Endangered Species Act's existing protections stayed intact because the Senate never acted; developers, agricultural interests, and water and power users who backed the rollback got nothing, and no taxpayer-funded compensation program was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing species protections; industry backers gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split mainly by party: 193 of 230 Republicans voted yes and 158 of 202 Democrats voted no, with 36 Democrats and 34 Republicans breaking ranks; 96 members of both parties had cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill repeals critical habitat designation, tells the Secretary to list species only sparingly, and pays owners for development the Act blocks. Those changes remove the main brake on building in the habitat of protected species, which is what the public loses when a species' home can be paved.

Any pesticide use that complies with pesticide-registration law is deemed automatically compliant with the Endangered Species Act, ending separate review of pesticide harms to listed species, and ranchers get reimbursed for livestock lost to reintroduced predators.

industries.industry: Western water users and federal power customers (hydropower and irrigation interests)
industries.note: Jeopardy analyses would count only impacts beyond a baseline of past harm, mitigation must be roughly proportional, and operators of dams and canals are exempted from liability for harm to aquatic species caused by state fishing programs. Federal power administrations would simply have to print each customer's share of Endangered Species Act compliance costs on their bills.

Landowners could receive conservation grants, annual payments covering up to 100% of their costs under multi-year contracts, and compensation for foregone development. Those payments would come from taxpayers, so landowners' gain is the public's cost.

The bill repeals critical habitat authority, raises the bar for listings, and caps mitigation, shrinking the tools available to recover listed species. The transparency, recovery-plan deadlines, and landowner incentives it adds do not offset the loss of habitat protection.
